title: IgE Biology, Units, Omalizumab and Alpha-Gal Syndrome
summary: Learn the properties that make IgE scarce in serum yet potent on mast cells, how IgE results are standardized and converted, how omalizumab is dosed and why total IgE rises on it, and how alpha-gal IgE causes delayed meat reactions and cetuximab anaphylaxis.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 56 Hits 2 (total IgE calibration), 3 (IgE biology), 4 (FcεRI affinity), 9 (alpha-gal syndrome) and 10 (omalizumab), checked against Ansotegui 2020 (WAO), Hu 2018, Sutton 2019, Plattner 2023, Nagata 2022, Thomson 2012, Menzella 2023, Zhu 2024, Macdougall 2022, Vaz-Rodrigues 2022 and Chung 2008 (read via a page-fetch tool). Corrections and qualifications: cetuximab reaction rate (22% in the cited southeastern series, not “up to 1/3”); omalizumab free-IgE goal (about 25 ng/mL, not 25 kU/L); US paediatric IgE range up to 1300 IU/mL; heat inactivation time (4 h at 56 °C in Hu 2018); IgE can reach the fetus inside IgG anti-IgE complexes. Not taught as facts: 18% carbohydrate, interlaboratory CV <15%, 40,000–500,000 receptors and ~1000 cross-links per cell. The Number Vault (table1) is not claimed because not every row is taught.

objectives: Describe the serum properties of IgE (size, abundance, half-life, complement, FcRn) and its affinity for FcεRI.
Convert total IgE between international units and mass and state the standard it is traceable to.
Explain how omalizumab works, how it is dosed, and why total IgE rises during treatment.
Recognize alpha-gal syndrome and its link to tick bites, delayed meat reactions and cetuximab.

scenes.title: Three IgE puzzles
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: three items reach the immunology bench — (1) a total IgE result of 200 kU/L and a clinician asking “how much is that in micrograms per litre?”; (2) a patient on omalizumab whose total IgE is now HIGHER than before treatment; (3) a man with hives and low blood pressure about 4 hours after a steak dinner, who reports several recent tick bites. Question token: “Units, drug, or sugar?”

cues.text: Three puzzles reach the bench. A total IgE of two hundred kilounits per litre, and a request to express it by mass.
A patient on the anti-IgE drug omalizumab whose total IgE has gone up, not down. And hives and low blood pressure four hours after a steak, in a man with recent tick bites.
Is each one about units, about the drug, or about a sugar?

scenes.title: A rare antibody with a tight grip
scenes.altText: Schematic IgE molecule and a mast cell. Card “IgE in serum”: about 190 kDa, sedimentation coefficient 8S; the least abundant isotype (about 150 ng/mL vs about 10 mg/mL for IgG in one review); serum half-life about 1.5–3 days vs about 20 days (2–3 weeks) for IgG, partly because IgE does not bind FcRn; IgE alone does not activate complement. Card “On the cell”: FcεRI binds the Cε3 region of IgE with Ka ≈ 10¹⁰ M⁻¹, at least 100-fold higher than IgG for its receptors; most IgE is already cell-bound and stays there for weeks; cross-linking very few IgE–FcεRI complexes triggers degranulation; serum IgE level drives FcεRI expression.

cues.text: IgE is the scarcest antibody in serum. It is a glycoprotein of about one hundred and ninety kilodaltons, eight S, at roughly one hundred and fifty nanograms per millilitre, against about ten milligrams per millilitre of IgG.

Free IgE is short-lived: a serum half-life of about one and a half to three days, against about three weeks for IgG, partly because IgE does not bind the recycling receptor FcRn. And IgE alone does not activate complement.

Its strength is its grip. The high-affinity receptor FcεRI holds the Cε3 region of IgE with an affinity constant of about ten to the tenth per molar, at least a hundred times tighter than IgG holds its receptors.

So most IgE sits on mast cells and basophils for weeks, and cross-linking only a few of those IgE–receptor pairs is enough to release mediators. Serum IgE level also drives how much FcεRI the cell expresses.

scenes.title: Units, then the anti-IgE drug
scenes.altText: Card “Units”: commercial total IgE assays are cross-standardized to the WHO human IgE standard 11/234; results are reported in IU/mL (equivalent to kU/L); a conversion factor of 1 IU = 2.42 ng is sometimes applied, so 1 kU/L ≈ 2.42 µg/L; specific IgE is reported as kUA/L. Card “Omalizumab”: humanized anti-IgE that binds the Cε3 domain of FREE IgE, blocking FcεRI binding; it cannot bind IgE already on FcεRI; FcεRI expression falls with treatment. Card “Dosing”: by baseline total IgE and body weight from a dosing table; subcutaneous every 2 or 4 weeks; US: 30–700 IU/mL for age ≥12 (up to 1300 IU/mL for ages 6–<12); EU: up to 1500 IU/mL; original goal: mean free IgE about 25 ng/mL or less.

cues.text: Total IgE assays are cross-standardized to the WHO human IgE standard, eleven slash two three four. Results come in international units per millilitre, the same as kilounits per litre, and one unit is about two point four two nanograms.

Omalizumab is a humanized antibody against IgE. It binds the Cε3 region of free IgE, the same site the receptor uses, so IgE cannot load onto mast cells. It cannot grab IgE already on the receptor, and receptor numbers fall during treatment.

It is dosed from a table using baseline total IgE and body weight, given under the skin every two or four weeks. The US table covers thirty to seven hundred units per millilitre from age twelve, up to thirteen hundred for children six to under twelve; the EU table goes to fifteen hundred.
The original trials aimed to cut mean free IgE to about twenty-five nanograms per millilitre or less. Dosing uses the baseline value, before the drug starts.

props.title: Dosing table
lines: Baseline IgE + weight · SC every 2 or 4 weeks

props.label: Goal: free IgE ≈ 25 ng/mL or less

scenes.title: A sugar allergen, then the answers
scenes.altText: Card “Alpha-gal syndrome”: IgE against the sugar galactose-α-1,3-galactose rather than a protein; sensitization mostly follows tick bites (lone star tick, Amblyomma americanum, in the southeastern US); reactions to mammalian meat typically 3–6 hours after eating, unlike the minutes of protein food allergy. Card “Cetuximab”: the anticancer antibody carries alpha-gal on the Fab portion of its heavy chain (made in a mouse cell line); pre-existing alpha-gal IgE causes immediate reactions — severe hypersensitivity in 22% of treated patients in Tennessee and North Carolina in one study vs <1% at most northeastern centers. Card “Diagnosis”: alpha-gal-specific IgE supports the diagnosis with a consistent history; sensitization alone is not disease (in one German cohort only 8.6% with ≥0.35 kU/L had symptomatic meat allergy). Hook answers: (1) 200 kU/L × 2.42 ≈ 484 µg/L; (2) total IgE counts free plus drug-bound IgE, so it rises on omalizumab; (3) alpha-gal IgE with a tick history.

cues.text: Alpha-gal syndrome is IgE against a sugar, galactose alpha one three galactose, not a protein. Sensitization usually follows tick bites; in the southeastern US the lone star tick. Reactions to mammalian meat typically come three to six hours after eating.

The same sugar sits on the Fab portion of the cancer drug cetuximab, so people with alpha-gal IgE can react at the first infusion: twenty-two percent severe reactions in one Tennessee and North Carolina series, under one percent at most northeastern centres.

Alpha-gal IgE supports the diagnosis only with a matching history: many sensitized people never react. Back to the hook: two hundred kilounits per litre is about four hundred and eighty-four micrograms per litre.
On omalizumab, total IgE adds free IgE and drug-bound IgE, so it rises and does not show failure. And the steak reaction points to alpha-gal IgE, with the tick history as the clue.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Total IgE rose on omalizumab, so the drug failed” (✓ total IgE includes drug-bound IgE; it rises during treatment); “A reaction hours after eating cannot be IgE-mediated” (✓ alpha-gal IgE reactions to mammalian meat are typically delayed 3–6 hours); “IgE fixes complement and lasts like IgG” (✓ IgE alone does not activate complement; serum half-life about 1.5–3 days vs about 3 weeks for IgG).

cues.text: Trap one: total IgE rose on omalizumab, so the drug failed. No: the assay counts drug-bound IgE too, and total IgE rises during treatment.
Trap two: a reaction hours after a meal cannot be IgE-mediated. No: alpha-gal reactions to red meat are IgE-mediated and typically start three to six hours later.
Trap three: IgE behaves like IgG. No: IgE alone does not activate complement, and its serum half-life is days, not weeks.

scenes.title: Scarce, sticky, sugar-tagged
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “IgE is SCARCE in serum, STICKY on the mast cell, and can be SUGAR-TAGGED. Omalizumab HANDCUFFS the free ones, so the handcuffed ones still get counted.” Tokens: scarce = short half-life, lowest level · sticky = Ka ≈ 10¹⁰ · sugar = alpha-gal · handcuffs = omalizumab–IgE complexes in total IgE. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: IgE is scarce in serum, sticky on the mast cell, and can be sugar-tagged. Omalizumab handcuffs the free molecules, and the handcuffed ones still get counted in total IgE.

Where it breaks: IgE on cells lasts weeks, so scarce in serum is not short-lived in tissue; alpha-gal is the sugar the IgE recognizes, not a tag on IgE itself; and whether a total IgE assay detects drug-bound IgE depends on the method.

props.title: Where it breaks
lines: Alpha-gal is the allergen, not on IgE

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “IgE: scarce, short serum life, Ka ≈ 10¹⁰ · units traceable to WHO 11/234, 1 IU ≈ 2.42 ng”, “Omalizumab: dose from baseline IgE and weight; total IgE rises on treatment · alpha-gal: tick bites, meat reactions 3–6 h, cetuximab”.

cues.text: IgE is scarce and short-lived in serum but grips its mast-cell receptor extremely tightly, so report it in WHO-traceable units, dose omalizumab from the baseline level because total IgE rises on treatment, and suspect alpha-gal when red meat or cetuximab triggers a reaction after tick bites.

props.label: Scarce · days · Ka ≈ 10¹⁰ · WHO 11/234 · 1 IU ≈ 2.42 ng
Omalizumab: baseline IgE + weight · alpha-gal: ticks, meat 3–6 h, cetuximab

explanation.what: Plain language: IgE is the rarest antibody in blood and does not last long there, but it sticks so tightly to mast cells that a little allergen can set them off. Labs report it in standardized units; the anti-IgE drug omalizumab mops up the free IgE; and one unusual allergy, alpha-gal, is IgE against a sugar found in red meat and in the drug cetuximab. Scientific terms: immunoglobulin E, FcεRI, affinity constant (Ka), Cε3 domain, FcRn, WHO IgE standard 11/234, IU/mL, kU/L, kUA/L, omalizumab, free vs total IgE, galactose-α-1,3-galactose, Amblyomma americanum, cetuximab Fab.
explanation.why: Because IgE binds FcεRI so tightly, most IgE sits on effector cells and only a few cross-links are needed to trigger them. Omalizumab binds the receptor-binding Cε3 site on free IgE, so free IgE falls while drug–IgE complexes accumulate and total IgE rises. Alpha-gal IgE is made after tick bites; the sugar in meat reaches the circulation slowly, so reactions are delayed, while the sugar on intravenous cetuximab triggers immediate reactions.
explanation.measure: Total IgE: IU/mL (= kU/L), cross-standardized to WHO 11/234; 1 IU ≈ 2.42 ng (so 1 kU/L ≈ 2.42 µg/L). Omalizumab: dose by baseline total IgE and body weight; SC every 2 or 4 weeks; US 30–700 IU/mL (age ≥12) and up to 1300 IU/mL (6–<12); EU up to 1500 IU/mL; trial goal mean free IgE ≈25 ng/mL or less. Alpha-gal: serum alpha-gal-specific IgE (beef thyroglobulin or cetuximab as the alpha-gal source) supports diagnosis with a consistent history.
explanation.differs: Free IgE vs total IgE (free + drug-bound); serum IgE (days) vs cell-bound IgE (weeks); IgE (no complement, no FcRn) vs IgG; alpha-gal meat reactions (delayed 3–6 h) vs protein food allergy (minutes) vs cetuximab reactions (immediate).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: a unit conversion, the reason total IgE rises on omalizumab, the omalizumab IgE eligibility range, the cause of delayed red-meat anaphylaxis after tick bites, or why cetuximab can cause first-dose anaphylaxis.

mnemonic.text: IgE is SCARCE in serum, STICKY on the mast cell, and can meet a SUGAR allergen. Omalizumab HANDCUFFS the free ones, and the handcuffed ones still get counted.
mnemonic.explanation: Scarce = lowest level and short serum half-life; sticky = Ka ≈ 10¹⁰ M⁻¹; sugar = alpha-gal; handcuffs = omalizumab–IgE complexes included in total IgE.
mnemonic.limitation: Cell-bound IgE persists for weeks, so “scarce” applies to serum only; alpha-gal is the allergen recognized by IgE, not a tag on IgE itself; how a total IgE assay detects drug-bound IgE depends on the method.

Omalizumab dosing ranges are from US and EU labels as summarized in reviews; local labels may differ.
takeaway: IgE is scarce and short-lived in serum but grips its mast-cell receptor extremely tightly, so report it in WHO-traceable units, dose omalizumab from the baseline level because total IgE rises on treatment, and suspect alpha-gal when red meat or cetuximab triggers a reaction after tick bites.

questions.stem: A total IgE is reported as 150 kU/L. Using the conversion factor 1 IU ≈ 2.42 ng, what is the approximate mass concentration?

options.rationale: Correct. 1 kU/L = 1 IU/mL ≈ 2.42 ng/mL = 2.42 µg/L, so 150 × 2.42 ≈ 363 µg/L.
Incorrect. This divides by 2.42 instead of multiplying.
Incorrect. The factor is nanograms per unit, giving micrograms per litre, not milligrams.

options.text: It cannot be converted because IgE has no international standard
options.rationale: Incorrect. Commercial total IgE assays are cross-standardized to the WHO human IgE standard 11/234.

questions.stem: Three months after starting omalizumab, a patient’s serum total IgE is higher than before treatment, and the asthma is better controlled. What is the best explanation?

options.text: Total IgE includes omalizumab-bound IgE, which accumulates during treatment while free IgE falls
options.rationale: Correct. Reviews describe total IgE (free plus omalizumab-bound) rising during treatment while free IgE is reduced.

options.text: The drug has failed and the dose should be recalculated from this new value
options.rationale: Incorrect. A rise in total IgE is expected; the dosing table is based on baseline IgE.

options.text: Omalizumab stimulates B cells to make more IgE
options.rationale: Incorrect. The rise reflects drug–IgE complexes, not increased production.

options.text: The specimen must have been haemolysed
options.rationale: Incorrect. Nothing suggests a pre-analytical error; the pattern is the expected drug effect.

questions.stem: A patient from the southeastern United States with a history of hives several hours after eating beef is about to receive cetuximab. Why is the oncology team concerned?

options.text: Cetuximab carries galactose-α-1,3-galactose on its Fab, so pre-existing alpha-gal IgE can cause immediate anaphylaxis
options.rationale: Correct. Chung 2008 found IgE to the alpha-gal oligosaccharide on the cetuximab heavy-chain Fab in pretreatment samples from most patients who reacted.

options.text: Cetuximab contains beef protein that cross-reacts with meat allergens
options.rationale: Incorrect. The shared allergen is a sugar, not a beef protein; the drug is made in a mouse cell line that adds alpha-gal.

options.text: Any reaction to cetuximab will also be delayed by 3–6 hours
options.rationale: Incorrect. The delay applies to eaten meat; infused cetuximab causes immediate reactions.

options.text: Alpha-gal IgE blocks the anticancer effect of cetuximab
options.rationale: Incorrect. The concern is hypersensitivity, not loss of efficacy.

claims.text: IgE ~190 kDa, 8S, lowest serum isotype; serum half-life ~1.5–3 days vs ~3 weeks for IgG; no FcRn binding; IgE alone does not activate complement.
FcεRI binds IgE Cε3 with Ka ≈ 10¹⁰ M⁻¹ (≥100× IgG–FcγR); most IgE cell-bound for weeks; few cross-links trigger release; FcεRI tracks serum IgE.
Total IgE cross-standardized to WHO 11/234; IU/mL = kU/L; 1 IU ≈ 2.42 ng.
Omalizumab binds Cε3 of free IgE, cannot bind receptor-bound IgE, downregulates FcεRI; total IgE (free + bound) rises during treatment.
Dose by baseline IgE and weight; SC every 2 or 4 weeks; US 30–700 IU/mL (≥12 y), ≤1300 (6–<12 y); EU ≤1500 IU/mL; goal free IgE ≈25 ng/mL or less.

Alpha-gal syndrome: IgE to a sugar; tick-bite sensitization (lone star tick, southeastern US); meat reactions typically 3–6 h; diagnosis by history plus alpha-gal sIgE; sensitization alone is not disease.
Alpha-gal on the cetuximab heavy-chain Fab; pretreatment IgE in most reactors; 22% severe reactions in Tennessee/North Carolina vs <1% in most northeastern centres.

IgE 18% carbohydrate; interlaboratory CV <15%; 40,000–500,000 FcεRI per cell and ~1000 cross-linked IgE needed; skin-sensitizing activity destroyed by 56 °C for 2 hours; cetuximab reactions in up to one-third.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 56 Hit 9 says the alpha-gal epitope on cetuximab causes reactions in “up to 1/3 of treated patients”. Chung 2008 reports severe hypersensitivity in 22% of patients treated in Tennessee and North Carolina (<1% at most northeastern centres, 3% on the label), and Macdougall 2022 gives <3% globally and up to 22% in the southeastern US; the lesson teaches the sourced figures (register flag rv-cetuximab-reaction-rate).

Ch. 56 Hit 10 says omalizumab drives free IgE below “~25 kU/L” (the Memory Hook says <50 ng/mL, ~25 kU/L). Zhu 2024 states the pivotal-trial goal was mean free IgE of about 25 ng/mL or less; at 2.42 ng per IU, 25 ng/mL is about 10 IU/mL and 50 ng/mL about 21 IU/mL, so “25 kU/L” mixes units (register flag rv-omalizumab-free-ige-units).

Ch. 56 Hit 10 gives US omalizumab eligibility as 30–700 kU/L. Menzella 2023 and Zhu 2024 state 700 IU/mL is the US maximum for age ≥12, while the US paediatric table (6–<12 years) extends to 1300 IU/mL (register flag rv-omalizumab-us-paediatric-range).

Ch. 56 Hit 3 says IgE skin-sensitizing activity is destroyed by 56 °C for 2 hours. Hu 2018 states IgE loses its binding ability after 4 h at 56 °C; the lesson does not teach a heating time (register flag rv-ige-heat-inactivation-time).

Ch. 56 Hit 3 says IgE has no placental transfer. IgE does not bind FcRn (Sutton 2019), but Plattner 2023 cites evidence that maternal IgE can cross the placenta inside IgG anti-IgE/IgE immune complexes via FcRn (register flag rv-ige-placental-complexes).
Omalizumab eligibility ranges and dosing tables are US (FDA) and EU (EMA) label content as summarized in reviews; Philippine labelling and reimbursement rules are not covered.
